title: 26 U.S. Code Section 41(c)(1) Base Amount
description: Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(1), the credit's base amount is the fixed-base percentage times average gross receipts for the four prior years, with a 50% floor.

body.text: Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(1), the federal R&D tax credit base amount equals a taxpayer's fixed-base percentage times its average annual gross receipts for the four prior tax years. Businesses claiming the Regular Research Credit receive a 20 percent credit only on qualified research expenses above this base, which can never fall below 50 percent of current-year expenses.

Under 26 U.S. Code (U.S.C.) § 41(c)(1), the federal "base amount" for the Credit for Increasing Research Activities—commonly referred to as the Research and Development (R&D) tax credit—is the statutory performance benchmark defined as the product of a taxpayer's fixed-base percentage and its average annual gross receipts for the four taxable years preceding the credit year. Functioning as the mathematical core of the Regular Research Credit (RRC) under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) § 41(a)(1), the base amount ensures that the 20 percent federal credit applies strictly to incremental Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) that exceed a dynamically scaled baseline of historical research intensity, subject to a statutory floor under IRC § 41(c)(2) mandating that the base amount can never be less than 50 percent of current-year QREs.

body.text: Legislative Evolution and Statutory Mechanics of 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(1)
The Macroeconomic Principle of Incrementalism and OBRA '89 Restructuring

The federal Credit for Increasing Research Activities, codified at 26 U.S.C. § 41, is designed around the fiscal principle of incrementalism. Rather than subsidizing all baseline research and development expenditures that a business would incur in the ordinary course of operations, Congress structured the statute to reduce the marginal cost of capital specifically for incremental increases in research spending above an established historical benchmark. Under the general rule of 26 U.S.C. § 41(a)(1), a taxpayer's research credit for the taxable year equals 20 percent of the excess (if any) of the taxpayer's qualified research expenses (QREs) for the taxable year over the base amount—in addition to 20 percent of basic research payments determined under § 41(e)(1)(A) (per § 41(a)(2)) and 20 percent of amounts paid or incurred to an energy research consortium (per § 41(a)(3)).

When the research and experimentation tax credit first entered the Internal Revenue Code on a temporary basis in 1981, former IRC § 41(c)(1)–(2) defined the threshold as "base period research expenses," calculated as a rolling three-year average of the taxpayer's actual QREs from the three taxable years immediately preceding the credit year. As documented in the legislative history to the Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1989 (OBRA '89, Pub. L. 101-239, § 7110, 103 Stat. 2106, enacted December 19, 1989; H.R. Rep. No. 101-247, at 1199–1200) and examined in IRS Technical Advice Memorandum (TAM) 201740018, Congress recognized a structural flaw in the rolling three-year QRE average: a taxpayer that expanded its R&D spending in Year 1 automatically inflated its base period hurdle for Years 2, 3, and 4, eroding the incentive to sustain elevated research investment.

To eliminate this self-penalizing feedback loop while retaining an incremental credit structure that avoids subsidizing research that would have been undertaken in any event, OBRA '89 eliminated the terms "base period research expenses" and "base period" in § 41(a)(1) and (c) and replaced them with the modern "base amount" under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(1). Because businesses commonly determine research budgets as a fixed percentage of revenue, Congress indexed each taxpayer's base amount to its historical ratio of QREs to gross receipts (the "fixed-base percentage") scaled by average growth in gross receipts over the four preceding taxable years.
The Core Base Amount Formula and Fixed-Base Percentage (IRC § 41(c)(1) & (3))
Pursuant to 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(1), the term "base amount" is defined algebraically as the product of two statutory components:

Specifically, 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(1)(A) and (B) multiply the taxpayer's fixed-base percentage (FBP) by the average annual gross receipts of the taxpayer for the four taxable years preceding the taxable year for which the credit is being determined (statutorily designated in § 41(c)(1)(B) as the "credit year"). By coupling a fixed historical research-intensity ratio to a rolling four-year revenue average, the formula scales the taxpayer's expected baseline R&D expenditure in direct proportion to its recent revenue footprint without penalizing current-year QRE expansion.

For established corporate taxpayers that were active during the mid-1980s, 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(A) defines the fixed-base percentage as the percentage which the aggregate QREs of the taxpayer for taxable years beginning after December 31, 1983, and before January 1, 1989 (the 1984–1988 base period), is of the aggregate gross receipts of the taxpayer for those same taxable years. To prevent historically R&D-intensive enterprises from facing an insurmountable base hurdle as their revenues scale, Congress imposed two strict mathematical boundaries on the FBP computation under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(C) and (D): first, under § 41(c)(3)(C), in no event shall the fixed-base percentage exceed 16 percent (16.00%); and second, under § 41(c)(3)(D), all fixed-base percentages determined under subparagraphs (A) (existing taxpayers) and (B)(ii) (start-up taxpayers) must be rounded to the nearest one-hundredth of one percent (0.01%).
Start-Up Company Definition and Phase-In Mechanics (IRC § 41(c)(3)(B))

Because businesses formed after the mid-1980s—as well as existing businesses that did not simultaneously generate revenue and incur QREs during the mid-1980s—lack a representative 1984–1988 operational baseline, 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(B)(i) establishes specialized "start-up company" rules. A taxpayer is statutorily classified as a start-up company under § 41(c)(3)(B)(i)(I)–(II) if either (I) the first taxable year in which the taxpayer had both gross receipts and qualified research expenses begins after December 31, 1983, or (II) there are fewer than three taxable years beginning after December 31, 1983, and before January 1, 1989, in which the taxpayer had both gross receipts and qualified research expenses. As noted in Section 3.a of the IRS Audit Techniques Guide (ATG), a newly spun-off corporation is not automatically treated as a start-up company if it carries over relevant 1984–1988 base-year QREs and gross receipts from its predecessor under the acquisition and disposition rules of IRC § 41(f)(3). Furthermore, under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(B)(iii) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-3(c)(2)(vi) (promulgated in T.D. 8930), de minimis gross receipts received by a taxpayer in a taxable year preceding the first taxable year in which the taxpayer derives more than $25,000 in gross receipts other than investment income—defined as interest or distributions with respect to stock other than stock of a 20-percent owned corporation under IRC § 243(c)(2)—are excluded from gross receipts, preventing nominal early-stage revenue from prematurely triggering the start-up clock.

Under clause (I), the fixed-base percentage is fixed at 3 percent (3.00%) for each of the taxpayer's first five taxable years beginning after December 31, 1993, for which the taxpayer has qualified research expenses (only taxable years in which the taxpayer actually incurs QREs are counted in this sequence). Rather than a ten-year transition after Year 5, clauses (II) through (VI) establish a five-year phase-in transition spanning Years 6 through 10 (completing a 10-year initial window in total) that applies progressively increasing fractions (1/6, 1/3, 1/2, 2/3, and 5/6) to the ratio of aggregate QREs to aggregate gross receipts from specified prior post-1993 QRE years: in the 6th such year, 1/6 of the ratio for the 4th and 5th years; in the 7th year, 1/3 of the ratio for the 5th and 6th years; in the 8th year, 1/2 of the ratio for the 5th, 6th, and 7th years; in the 9th year, 2/3 of the ratio for the 5th, 6th, 7th, and 8th years; and in the 10th year, 5/6 of the ratio for the 5th, 6th, 7th, 8th, and 9th years. Finally, under clause (VII), for the 11th such taxable year and all subsequent years, the FBP is the percentage which the aggregate QREs for any five taxable years selected by the taxpayer from among the 5th through the 10th such taxable years is of the aggregate gross receipts of the taxpayer for such selected years, subject to the 16.00 percent maximum cap and 0.01 percent rounding rules under § 41(c)(3)(C)–(D).

body.text: The 50 Percent Minimum Base Amount Floor (IRC § 41(c)(2))

To protect federal tax revenues against sharp contractions in gross receipts or unusually low fixed-base percentages, 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(2) establishes an unconditional statutory floor: "In no event shall the base amount be less than 50 percent of the qualified research expenses for the credit year."

Consequently, the effective base amount governing any Regular Research Credit claim is the greater of (1) the product of the taxpayer's fixed-base percentage and prior four-year average annual gross receipts under § 41(c)(1), or (2) 50 percent of the taxpayer's credit-year QREs under § 41(c)(2). Without this 50 percent minimum floor, a corporation experiencing a severe revenue contraction—or a pre-revenue start-up with zero prior gross receipts under 26 CFR § 1.41-3(a)—would compute a preliminary base amount approaching or equal to $0, allowing the 20 percent RRC rate to apply to nearly 100 percent of its current-year QREs. By enforcing the 50 percent floor under § 41(c)(2), Congress guaranteed that no taxpayer claiming the Regular Research Credit can ever include more than half of its credit-year QREs in "excess QREs," capping the maximum effective federal RRC yield at 10 percent (20% multiplied by 50%) of total current-year QREs.
Executive Branch Interpretation: Treasury Regulations and IRS Enforcement
Definition, Exclusions, and Sourcing of Gross Receipts (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-3(c) & IRC § 41(c)(6))

Because "gross receipts" functions both as the denominator of the historical fixed-base percentage and as the four-year multiplier for the current credit year, its calculation is a primary focal point of IRS examinations—often having a greater impact on audit results than adjustments to credit-year QREs. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(6) (redesignated from § 41(c)(7) by Pub. L. 115-141, § 101(c)(2)), the statute specifies that gross receipts for any taxable year are reduced by returns and allowances made during the taxable year. Expanding upon this statutory framework, 26 CFR § 1.41-3(c)(1) defines gross receipts broadly as "the total amount, as determined under the taxpayer's method of accounting, derived by the taxpayer from all its activities and from all sources (e.g., revenues derived from the sale of inventory before reduction for cost of goods sold)."

In Section 3.b and Section 3.d of the IRS Audit Techniques Guide: Credit for Increasing Research Activities (i.e. Research Tax Credit) IRC § 41 — Research Credit Computation (ATG), examiners are instructed that when a taxpayer includes only net trade sales from Form 1120, line 1c, it understates its gross receipts. Instead, Section 3.d of the ATG directs examiners to begin income verification at Form 1120, page 1, line 11 (Total Income), adding back cost of goods sold (since gross receipts are not reduced by cost of goods sold) and including tax-exempt interest and other tax-exempt income (Selected Issues #3 and #4 of ATG Section 3.d). From that aggregate figure, 26 CFR § 1.41-3(c)(2)(i)–(vi) mandates the exclusion of six specific categories of receipts so that non-operating or pass-through items do not distort the taxpayer's economic scale:

items: Returns or allowances (26 CFR § 1.41-3(c)(2)(i)).
Capital asset dispositions: Receipts from the sale or exchange of capital assets, as defined in IRC § 1221 (26 CFR § 1.41-3(c)(2)(ii)).
Loan principal repayments: Repayments of loans or similar instruments, such as the repayment of the principal amount of a loan held by a commercial lender (26 CFR § 1.41-3(c)(2)(iii)).

Extraordinary dispositions outside the ordinary course of business: Receipts from a sale or exchange not in the ordinary course of business, such as the sale of an entire trade or business or the sale of property used in a trade or business as defined under IRC § 1221(2) (26 CFR § 1.41-3(c)(2)(iv)).

Collected sales and local taxes: Amounts received with respect to sales tax or other similar state and local taxes if, under the applicable state or local law, the tax is legally imposed on the purchaser of the good or service, and the taxpayer merely collects and remits the tax to the taxing authority (26 CFR § 1.41-3(c)(2)(v)).

Pre-$25,000 de minimis early-stage receipts: Amounts received by a taxpayer in a taxable year that precedes the first taxable year in which the taxpayer derives more than $25,000 in gross receipts other than investment income, where investment income is interest or distributions with respect to stock other than the stock of a 20-percent owned corporation as defined in IRC § 243(c)(2) (26 CFR § 1.41-3(c)(2)(vi)).

body.text: For multinational enterprises, geographic sourcing rules bifurcate sharply between foreign corporations and domestic corporations. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(6) and 26 CFR § 1.41-3(c)(3), in the case of a foreign corporation, gross receipts include only gross receipts that are effectively connected with the conduct of a trade or business within the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico (for amounts incurred after June 30, 1999), or other possessions of the United States (see IRC § 864(c)). Conversely, for a United States-domiciled corporation, the gross receipts of an unincorporated foreign branch must be included in the worldwide gross receipts calculation regardless of where the revenue is generated. Section 3.d of the IRS ATG (Selected Issue #1) explicitly states that "A foreign branch of a United States company should have its receipts included as part of the gross receipts computation." This administrative requirement derives from the "all its activities and from all sources" mandate of 26 CFR § 1.41-3(c)(1) and was enforced by the U.S. Tax Court in Deere & Co. v. Commissioner, 133 T.C. 246 (133 T.C. No. 11, October 22, 2009), which held that a domestic corporation cannot exclude the gross receipts of its foreign branch operations when computing its prior four-year average annual gross receipts under IRC § 41(c).
The Consistency Requirement (IRC § 41(c)(5)(A) & Treas. Reg. § 1.41-3(d))

Congress repealed former paragraph (4) (Alternative Incremental Credit) in 2018 and redesignated former paragraphs (5), (6), and (7) as paragraphs (4), (5), and (6) (26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(5)(A), per Pub. L. 115-141, Div. U, Title I, § 101(c)(1)–(2), March 23, 2018). Thus, the consistency mandate—originally enacted by OBRA '89 as § 41(c)(4), later numbered § 41(c)(5) when 26 CFR § 1.41-3(d) was promulgated in 2001, and numbered § 41(c)(6)(A) between 2006 and 2018—is currently codified at 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(5)(A).

Substantively, 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(5)(A) and 26 CFR § 1.41-3(d)(1) mandate that in computing the research credit for taxable years beginning after December 31, 1989, the QREs and gross receipts taken into account in computing a taxpayer's fixed-base percentage and base amount "must be determined on a basis consistent with the definition of qualified research expenses and gross receipts for the credit year, without regard to the law in effect for the taxable years taken into account in computing the fixed-base percentage or the base amount." Crucially, both the statute and regulation specify that this consistency requirement applies even if the period for filing a claim for credit or refund has expired for any historical taxable year taken into account in computing the fixed-base percentage or the base amount. As the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit explained in Trinity Industries, Inc. v. United States, 757 F.3d 400, 411 (5th Cir. 2014) (cited in IRS TAM 201740018), the consistency rule "aims to ensure that the research tax credit due is not overstated or understated because the taxpayer inconsistently compares QREs in the base period years and the claim year."

Treasury Regulation § 1.41-3(d)(2) illustrates the bidirectional nature of the consistency mandate through two regulatory examples. In Example 1 (downward base adjustment for statutory narrowing), Taxpayer X, an accrual-method calendar-year taxpayer, computes its research credit for 2001 using the 1984–1988 fixed-base period, during which it originally reported $720x of aggregate QREs on Form 6765 ($100x in 1984, $120x in 1985, $150x in 1986, $180x in 1987, and $170x in 1988). Because the statutory definition of qualified research changed for taxable years beginning after December 31, 1985, applying the credit-year (2001) definition retroactively reduces X's 1984 and 1985 QREs to $80x and $100x, respectively, lowering aggregate 1984–1988 base-period QREs to $680x ($80x + $100x + $150x + $180x + $170x = $680x). Conversely, in Example 2 (upward base adjustment for expanded claiming methodology), if Taxpayer X claims a specific type of expenditure in its 2001 credit-year QREs that it had not previously treated as QREs during the 1984–1988 fixed-base period, X is required to adjust its 1984–1988 base-period QREs upward to include any similar expenditures incurred during 1984–1988, regardless of whether the refund statute of limitations has expired for those base years.

(Additionally, as confirmed in IRS TAM 201740018 and United Therapeutics Corp. v. Commissioner, 105 F.4th 183 (4th Cir. 2024), electing the orphan drug credit under IRC § 45C for qualified clinical testing expenses in a credit year requires excluding those expenses from credit-year QREs under § 45C(c)(1), while § 45C(c)(2) mandates that such expenses still be included in base-period research comparison figures under § 41(c).)
Short Taxable Years (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-3(b)) and Corporate Acquisitions (IRC § 41(f)(3))

When corporate formations, restructurings, or M&A transactions create short taxable years of fewer than 12 months, 26 CFR § 1.41-3(b)(1)–(3) prescribes three distinct rules using a monthly proration standard (in contrast to the Alternative Simplified Credit under 26 CFR § 1.41-9(c)(3), which prorates by days over 365):

items: Short Credit Year (26 CFR § 1.41-3(b)(1)): If the credit year itself is a short taxable year, the preliminary base amount determined under IRC § 41(c)(1) (but not the 50 percent minimum base amount under § 41(c)(2)) is modified by multiplying that amount by the number of months in the short taxable year and dividing the result by 12. Current-year QREs incurred during the short credit year are not annualized; only the § 41(c)(1) preliminary base amount is reduced before comparing it against 50 percent of actual short-period QREs.

Short Taxable Year Preceding the Credit Year (26 CFR § 1.41-3(b)(2)): If one or more of the four taxable years preceding the credit year is a short taxable year, the gross receipts for that abbreviated year are annualized—deemed to be equal to the gross receipts actually derived in that year multiplied by 12 and divided by the number of months in that short year—preventing a short prior year from artificially depressing the four-year average annual gross receipts.

No Short-Year Adjustment to Fixed-Base Percentage (26 CFR § 1.41-3(b)(3)): No adjustment shall be made on account of a short taxable year to the computation of a taxpayer's historical fixed-base percentage.

body.text: Furthermore, if a taxpayer has not been in existence for four full taxable years preceding the credit year, 26 CFR § 1.41-3(a) provides that average annual gross receipts are computed over the actual number of preceding taxable years for which the taxpayer has been in existence (or zero if the taxpayer has not been in existence for any previous taxable year).

To prevent corporations from manufacturing artificial incremental QRE spikes via mergers or asset purchases, 26 U.S.C. § 41(f)(3) governs the acquisition or disposition of the major portion of a trade or business (or the major portion of a separate unit thereof). When a taxpayer acquires a major portion of a trade or business, both the historical QREs and the historical gross receipts of the predecessor attributable to that acquired business must be integrated into the acquiring taxpayer's base amount and fixed-base percentage computations for the acquisition year and subsequent credit years. As Section 3.e(3) of the IRS ATG notes, a mere acquisition or disposition of corporate stock standing alone does not trigger § 41(f)(3), though controlled group aggregation rules under IRC § 41(f)(1) separately require all members of a controlled group to be treated as a single taxpayer when computing the base amount.
Regulatory Evolution of Qualified Research: T.D. 8930, T.D. 9104, and T.D. 9786

Because the consistency rule of IRC § 41(c)(5)(A) links historical base-period QREs directly to the credit-year definition of qualified research under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d), regulatory shifts in § 41(d) directly govern base amount calculations. Under § 41(d)(1), qualified research must satisfy a four-part test applied separately to each business component (any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used in the taxpayer's trade or business per § 41(d)(2)(B)):

items: Section 174 Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(A)): Expenditures must be eligible to be treated as expenses under IRC § 174 (incurred in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business to eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a product, where uncertainty exists if available information does not establish capability, method, or appropriate design per 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1)).

Technological Information Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(i)): Research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature (fundamentally relying on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science).

Business Component Purpose Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) & (d)(3)): The application of the research must be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer relating to a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality (excluding style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors under § 41(d)(3)(B)).
Process of Experimentation Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(C)): Substantially all of the research activities must constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose.

body.text: The regulatory interpretation of these four tests evolved across three landmark Treasury Decisions. First, Treasury Decision 8930 (66 FR 280, published January 3, 2001) promulgated final regulations on the base amount under 26 CFR § 1.41-3 (including the $25,000 de minimis gross receipts rule and consistency illustrations), but imposed a restrictive "discovery test" under § 1.41-4 stating that research was undertaken to discover information only if it sought knowledge that "exceeds, expands, or refines the common knowledge of skilled professionals in a particular field of science or engineering." Following widespread criticism from the taxpayer community, Treasury and the IRS issued Notice 2001-19 (January 31, 2001) and proposed regulations REG-112991-01 (66 FR 66362, December 26, 2001), eliminating the requirement to expand the common knowledge of skilled professionals.

Second, Treasury Decision 9104 (69 FR 22, published January 2, 2004, applicable to taxable years ending on or after December 31, 2003, with an IRS commitment not to challenge consistent positions for prior years) finalized 26 CFR § 1.41-4, confirming under § 1.41-4(a)(3) that "discovering information" does not require exceeding common professional knowledge or succeeding in developing the business component, but rather requires an intent to eliminate uncertainty regarding the capability or method for developing or improving a business component, or the appropriate design of that business component (with a utility patent under 35 U.S.C. § 151 serving as a conclusive safe harbor under § 1.41-4(a)(3)(iii)). Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i), a process of experimentation is defined as an evaluative process designed to evaluate one or more alternatives to achieve a result where capability, method, or appropriate design is uncertain at the outset of the taxpayer's research activities—involving identifying the uncertainty, identifying one or more alternatives intended to eliminate it, and conducting a process of evaluating those alternatives (through modeling, simulation, or a systematic trial-and-error methodology). Furthermore, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6) established the 80 percent "substantially all" rule: the process of experimentation requirement is satisfied only if 80 percent or more of a taxpayer's research activities with respect to a business component, measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis (and without regard to § 1.41-2(d)(2)), constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose under § 41(d)(3).

Third, T.D. 9104 explicitly removed and reserved § 1.41-4(c)(6). The final IUS regulations under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6) were promulgated twelve years later in Treasury Decision 9786 (81 FR 68299, 68306, published and effective October 4, 2016; 2016-42 I.R.B.). Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6), software is developed primarily for internal use only if it is developed for use in general and administrative functions that facilitate or support the conduct of the taxpayer's trade or business—specifically limited to financial management functions, human resources management functions, and support services functions (with a 25 percent safe harbor under § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi) for dual-function software subsets where third-party use is reasonably anticipated to constitute at least 10 percent of total use). Unless developed for use in an activity that itself constitutes qualified research, a qualified production process, or an integrated hardware-software product, internal use software must satisfy both the general four-part test of § 41(d)(1) and the three-part High Threshold of Innovation Test under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii): (1) the software is innovative (would result in a substantial and economically significant reduction in cost or improvement in speed or other measurable objective improvement); (2) the software development involves significant economic risk (the taxpayer commits substantial resources and there is substantial uncertainty, because of technical risk, that such resources would be recovered within a reasonable period); and (3) the software is not commercially available for use by the taxpayer without modifications that would satisfy the first two requirements.
Federal Judicial Interpretation: Substantiation, Estimation, and Sampling

Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(d), "A taxpayer claiming a credit under section 41 must retain records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that the expenditures claimed are eligible for the credit." Because reconstructing both current-year QREs and 1984–1988 base-period QREs under the consistency rule frequently collides with incomplete historical records, federal courts have delineated the boundary between permissible estimation and unsubstantiated conjecture.
The Cohan Estimation Doctrine: United States v. McFerrin, 570 F.3d 672 (5th Cir. 2009)

In United States v. McFerrin, 570 F.3d 672 (5th Cir. June 9, 2009), chemical engineer Arthur R. McFerrin (owner of four Subchapter S petrochemical corporations: KMCO, Inc., KMTEX, South Coast Acquisition, Inc., and South Coast Delaware, Inc.) filed an amended 1999 return in September 2003 claiming a $472,092.00 research credit under IRC § 41, resulting in an erroneous refund payment of $601,228.40 (including interest). When the United States sued in October 2005 to recover the refund, the district court ruled for the government after a six-day bench trial, applying pre-2003 case law requiring that research expand or refine existing scientific principles through formal hypothesis testing rather than "trial and error," and refusing to allow any credit because KMCO lacked contemporaneous written records of hours or supplies.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit vacated and remanded the judgment. First, the Fifth Circuit held that the district court erred by failing to apply the definitions promulgated in the December 2003 regulations (T.D. 9104 / 26 CFR § 1.41-4, which the government conceded applied), under which discovering technological information merely requires intending to eliminate uncertainty and a process of experimentation encompasses systematic trial-and-error evaluation of alternatives. Second, invoking the longstanding doctrine of Cohan v. Commissioner, 39 F.2d 540 (2d Cir. 1930), the Fifth Circuit held that if the taxpayer establishes on remand that qualified research activities actually occurred under the proper regulatory standard, the trial court must estimate the allowable expenses using available evidence—including employee testimony and institutional knowledge—rather than denying the credit in its entirety for lack of exact hour-by-hour documentation ("to allow nothing at all appears to us inconsistent with saying that something was spent"), while bearing heavily against the taxpayer whose inexactitude is of its own making.
The Evidentiary Floor for Estimation: Shami, Moore, Bayer Corp., Union Carbide, and Max

Subsequent federal litigation confirms that McFerrin and the Cohan rule do not excuse a taxpayer from establishing a credible evidentiary foundation. In Basim Shami and Rania Ardah, et al. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2012-78 (March 21, 2012), aff'd in part, 741 F.3d 560 (5th Cir. 2014), Farouk Systems, Inc. (FS), an S corporation manufacturing hair, skin, and nail care products (such as BioSilk and CHI), claimed approximately $1.5 million in research credits for tax years 2003–2005 based almost entirely on wages paid to its Founder/CEO/President Farouk Shami ($8,735,727 in 2003; $7,988,310 in 2004; $9,529,639 in 2005) and Executive Vice President John McCall ($5,722,699 in 2003 and $1,839,581 in 2004). Although FS maintained an R&D department of 18 to 27 staff and neither executive held formal education or training in science or engineering, petitioners claimed that both executives spent 80 percent of their time in 2003 and 2004 (seeking to treat 100 percent of their wages as QREs under the 80 percent "substantially all" wage rule of IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2)) and 35 percent / 30 percent of their time in 2005 performing qualified research services. The Tax Court disallowed 100 percent of the claimed executive wage QREs, finding the executives' uncorroborated, self-serving oral testimony contradicted by other witnesses and holding under Williams v. United States, 245 F.2d 559 (5th Cir. 1957), that the Cohan rule is inapplicable where the record provides no reasonable evidentiary basis upon which to base an estimate (which would otherwise amount to "unguided largesse").

Similarly, in Scott Moore and Gayla Moore v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-20, aff'd, No. 23-2681, 133 AFTR 2d 2024-1457 (7th Cir. April 30, 2024), the Seventh Circuit affirmed the disallowance of research credits claimed by the owner of Nevco, Inc. (an S corporation manufacturing scoreboards) that allocated 65 percent of the salary and bonuses of Nevco's President/COO (Gary Robert) to QREs. Under the "one-up" rule of 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(2), "direct supervision" means immediate first-line supervision of researchers, excluding a corporate president who supervised the Director of Engineering (who in turn supervised the engineers); moreover, because Robert kept no written task records under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(d) separating qualified experimentation from general new product development, the Tax Court and Seventh Circuit held it was impossible to calculate the incremental credit over the § 41(a)(1) base amount.

In Bayer Corp. & Subsidiaries v. United States, 850 F. Supp. 2d 522 (W.D. Pa. February 6, 2012), Bayer claimed approximately $175 million in R&D tax credits for 1990–2006 by aggregating expenses across more than 1,300 cost centers rather than identifying specific business components (which Bayer estimated exceeded 100,000 across 49 research sites). While IRS Revenue Procedure 2011-42 provides safe-harbor guidelines for using statistical sampling to estimate federal tax values when a full population frame of business components is established, Bayer moved the district court to impose a statistical sampling plan across 8 of its 49 research sites without first identifying all underlying business components. The district court denied Bayer's motion, holding that under IRC § 41(d)(2)(A) the four-part test must be applied separately to each business component, and that "a sampling plan that would not identify all of the business components underlying the claimed QRE credits is not acceptable in the absence of agreement by the Government" because it would improperly relieve the taxpayer of its burden of proof for the remaining 41 sites under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(d). (The U.S. Tax Court applied this same principle in Kapur v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-28 (March 12, 2024), declining to limit discovery to a sample of projects where the IRS sought discovery on the entire sampling frame.)

Finally, in Union Carbide Corp. & Subsidiaries v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2009-50, aff'd, 697 F.3d 104 (2d Cir. September 7, 2012), and Max v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-37, the courts examined the substantive boundaries of the four-part test that feeds into both base-period and credit-year QREs. In Union Carbide, addressing over $200 million in claimed costs across 106 plant process projects for 1994–1995, the Tax Court and Second Circuit confirmed that to satisfy § 41(d)(1)(C), research must follow a methodical plan involving a series of trials to test, analyze, refine, and retest a hypothesis; while the Tax Court accepted reasonable employee recollections and data extrapolations to estimate qualifying labor costs, both courts disallowed commercial production supply costs under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(2) that would have been purchased regardless of research to manufacture goods for sale (awarding only $1,045 of the >$200 million at issue). In Max v. Commissioner, disallowing R&D credits for apparel design and pattern-making, the Tax Court reinforced that qualifying uncertainty under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1) and § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) must concern technical capability, method, or appropriate design resolved through hard sciences (physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science) rather than style, cosmetic, business, or scheduling uncertainty.

body.text: State Conformity Frameworks and Base Amount Divergence

While state R&D tax credit statutes generally cross-reference the federal baseline of IRC § 41, state legislatures modify the base amount calculation in three fundamental ways: (1) adopting either static conformity (freezing IRC § 41 as of a specific historical date) or selective conformity; (2) restricting QREs strictly to research physically conducted within the state's geographic borders; and (3) redefining or eliminating the gross receipts multiplier in the base amount formula.

body.text: California: Revenue and Taxation Code (R&TC) § 23609

California's Research and Development Tax Credit, codified at Cal. R&TC § 23609 (for corporations under the Corporation Tax Law) and R&TC § 17052.12 (for individuals, partnerships, LLCs, and S-corporation pass-throughs under the Personal Income Tax Law) and claimed on Form FTB 3523, modifies the federal IRC § 41 framework through distinct credit rates, strict in-state research requirements, and a narrow, localized definition of gross receipts. Under Cal. R&TC § 23609(f), unused California research credits cannot be carried back, but may be carried forward indefinitely to succeeding years until exhausted. An S corporation may utilize one-third (1/3) of the allowable research credit against its entity-level tax (not below the $800 minimum franchise tax, with the remaining two-thirds disregarded at the corporate level), while 100 percent of the credit calculated under the Personal Income Tax Law passes through to its shareholders.

For taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2000, Cal. R&TC § 23609 modifies the federal 20 percent rates in IRC § 41(a)(1) and (a)(2) to establish a 15 percent California Regular Research Credit (RRC) on the excess of current-year California QREs over the California base amount, and a 24 percent California Basic Research Credit (BRC) for basic research payments determined under IRC § 41(e)(1)(A) paid pursuant to a written contract to statutorily defined Qualified Organizations (such as universities, scientific research organizations, and specialized laboratory cancer centers with National Cancer Institute Clinical Cancer Research Center status) for basic research conducted within California. California strictly enforces the federal 50 percent minimum base amount floor of IRC § 41(c)(2), ensuring that the California base amount can never be less than 50 percent of current-year California QREs (Form FTB 3523, Line 14).

Under Cal. R&TC § 23609(c)(2), "qualified research" and "basic research" include only research physically conducted in California, and R&TC § 23609(c)(1) excludes from QREs any amount paid or incurred for tangible personal property eligible for a sales and use tax exemption under R&TC § 6378. While older FTB manuals and OTA opinions cite former R&TC § 23609(h)(3), California's statutory amendment adding the Alternative Simplified Credit in subsection (h) redesignated the localized gross receipts definition to Cal. R&TC § 23609(i).

Substantively, Cal. R&TC § 23609(i) modifies IRC § 41(c)(6) to take into account only those gross receipts "from the sale of property held primarily for sale to customers in the ordinary course of the taxpayer's trade or business that is delivered or shipped to a purchaser within this state, regardless of f.o.b. point or any other condition of the sale" (including sales to the U.S. government delivered or shipped to a customer in California). As confirmed by the Form FTB 3523 instructions and the California Office of Tax Appeals in Appeal of Electronic Data Systems Corporation & Subsidiaries (2023-OTA-540, decided September 20, 2023), while "property" encompasses real, tangible, and intangible property held for sale (including actual sales of software to California customers), California law strictly excludes receipts from the sale of services, rents, operating leases, interest, royalties, licenses, and throwback sales (property shipped from California to out-of-state purchasers). This divergence creates a major compliance hazard for multistate taxpayers: if a taxpayer inadvertently uses its worldwide federal gross receipts (or general apportionment sales factor receipts) as the multiplier for its four-year average California gross receipts on Line 11 of Form FTB 3523, its California base amount will be severely overstated, artificially reducing or eliminating its 15 percent California credit.

Because California excludes service revenue, royalties, licensing fees, and out-of-state deliveries from research gross receipts, many California-based R&D performers—such as software-as-a-service (SaaS) companies, engineering service firms, and pharmaceutical licensors—incur substantial California QREs while recording zero California gross receipts. After briefly issuing and withdrawing Legal Division Guidance (LDG) 2011-06-01 in June–July 2011, the California Franchise Tax Board (FTB) issued Legal Division Guidance 2012-03-01 (LDG 2012-03-01) on March 1, 2012. Under LDG 2012-03-01, the Form FTB 3523 instructions, and FTB S Corporation Manual Chapter 12, three rules govern zero-gross-receipts taxpayers:

items: Eligibility for the Regular Research Credit: A taxpayer with California QREs but $0 in California gross receipts for the four preceding years (entering $0 on Form FTB 3523, Line 11) is permitted to claim the 15 percent Regular Research Credit.

Ineligibility for Alternative Incremental Credit & Mandatory Start-Up Treatment: A zero-gross-receipts taxpayer cannot elect the Alternative Incremental Credit (because an AIC base equal to 1%, 1.5%, or 2% of $0 gross receipts would be meaningless); instead, the taxpayer must compute the Regular Research Credit as a start-up company under Section A of Form FTB 3523. In the taxpayer's sixth year and beyond, if division by zero gross receipts makes a mathematical ratio impossible, the statutory language of IRC § 41(c)(3)(C) controls and the taxpayer must use a fixed-base percentage of 16 percent (0.16).

Governance of the 50 Percent Minimum Base Floor: Because multiplying either 3 percent or 16 percent by $0 average annual California gross receipts yields a preliminary base amount of $0, LDG 2012-03-01 mandates that the taxpayer calculate its base amount using the minimum base amount equal to 50 percent of current-year California QREs under IRC § 41(c)(2). Subtracting this 50 percent base floor from current-year California QREs leaves 50 percent as excess QREs, which at the 15 percent statutory rate yields an effective flat credit of 7.5 percent (15% × 50%) on total current-year California QREs.

body.text: Appeal of Pacific Coast Building Products, Inc. (Lead Case No. 514183, heard September 12, 2012, and October 29, 2013, and formally adopted February 25, 2014) was decided by the California State Board of Equalization (BOE). In Pacific Coast Building Products, the BOE evaluated R&TC § 23609 refund claims for a manufacturing enterprise, focusing on the fourth element of IRC § 41(d)—the Process of Experimentation Test under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) and the 80 percent "substantially all" rule—and ordered the refund claims granted for 90 percent of remaining claimed expenses after excluding $4,082,367 of non-eligible expenses across 18 projects that fell outside the project fiscal years. Following California's transfer of tax appeals jurisdiction to the Office of Tax Appeals (OTA), the OTA has enforced strict substantiation of base-period gross receipts under R&TC § 23609 and LDG 2012-03-01, notably in Appeal of Electronic Data Systems Corporation & Subsidiaries (2023-OTA-540, heard June 14, 2023, decided September 20, 2023), where the OTA denied an appellant's reliance on LDG 2012-03-01 because its original AIC refund claims failed to put FTB on notice of a Regular Research Credit claim and the appellant failed to substantiate that its $6.48 billion to $10.77 billion in annual net receipts contained zero California property or software sales.

Under R&TC § 23609(h)(1), for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2000, and before January 1, 2025, taxpayers could elect the former federal AIC under IRC § 41(c)(4) (as in effect on January 1, 2015) using California's modified three-tiered rates applied against four-year average California gross receipts: 1.49 percent on QREs exceeding 1.0% up to 1.5% of average gross receipts (Tier 1); 1.98 percent on QREs exceeding 1.5% up to 2.0% of average gross receipts (Tier 2); and 2.48 percent on QREs exceeding 2.0% of average gross receipts (Tier 3). However, under amended R&TC § 23609(h)(2), for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2025, California conforms to the federal Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) election under IRC § 41(c)(4), modifying the federal 14 percent rate in IRC § 41(c)(4)(A) to 3 percent (3.0%) of current-year California QREs exceeding 50 percent of average California QREs for the three preceding taxable years, and modifying the federal 6 percent fallback rate in IRC § 41(c)(4)(B)(ii) (where the taxpayer has no QREs in any one of the three preceding taxable years) to 1.3 percent of current-year California QREs.

body.text: Pennsylvania: Article XVII-B of the Tax Reform Code of 1971

Governed by Article XVII-B of the Tax Reform Code of 1971 (72 P.S. §§ 8702-B & 8703-B et seq.) and administered by the Pennsylvania Department of Revenue, the Pennsylvania Research and Development Tax Credit dispenses entirely with both the 1984–1988 fixed-base period and the gross receipts multiplier. Instead of indexing the base hurdle to gross receipts, Pennsylvania defines the "Pennsylvania base amount" exclusively by reference to historical in-state QREs, setting it equal to the greater of (1) 50 percent of the taxpayer's current-year Pennsylvania QREs, or (2) the average of the taxpayer's Pennsylvania QREs from the four immediately preceding taxable years. To qualify for the credit, an applicant must demonstrate at least two years of prior R&D expenditures conducted within Pennsylvania, maintain full state tax compliance (including any 20%+ owners), and file an annual electronic application via the Department of Revenue's myPATH portal between August 1 and December 1 for expenses incurred in the prior tax year (with awards issued by May 1).

Pennsylvania applies a bifurcated rate structure to excess Pennsylvania QREs over the Pennsylvania base amount: standard or large businesses receive a 10 percent credit rate, whereas a Qualified Small Business—defined as a for-profit business entity (corporation, LLC, or partnership) with a net book value of assets under $5,000,000 (documented via balance sheet) at the beginning or end of the taxable year—receives a doubled credit rate of 20 percent on excess Pennsylvania QREs. Pennsylvania imposes a statewide annual program cap of $60,000,000 (increased from an earlier $55,000,000 cap with an $11,000,000 small business reserve), of which $12,000,000 is statutorily reserved as a small business set-aside (if total applications exceed the cap, awards are prorated within the respective pools). Unused credits are nonrefundable and cannot be carried back, but may be carried forward by the original recipient for up to 15 succeeding taxable years. Crucially, approved recipients that cannot utilize their credits against their own qualified tax liabilities may apply (by June 1 following the award year) to sell or assign unused credits to third-party buyers on the open market (where buyers may offset up to 75 percent of their tax liability in the year of purchase with no carryforward or resale), with credits reported by tax advisory analyses to trade at approximately 92 to 93 cents on the dollar (averaging 92.9 percent of face value).
Indiana, Idaho, Arizona, New Jersey, Connecticut, and Rhode Island
The remaining state jurisdictions illustrate the spectrum of static conformity, geographic gross receipts sourcing, and modified base amount structures:

In Indiana (Indiana Code § 6-3.1-4) the state exemplifies static conformity. Under IC 6-3.1-4, both "Indiana qualified research expense" and the Indiana "base amount" (effective July 1, 2005) are defined by reference to IRC § 41(b) and § 41(c) as in effect on January 1, 2001, restricted strictly to research conducted in Indiana and gross receipts attributable to Indiana (subject to the 50 percent minimum base floor and 16 percent maximum FBP cap). This January 1, 2001 freeze date predates the publication of T.D. 8930 (January 3, 2001), T.D. 9104 (January 2, 2004), and T.D. 9786 (October 4, 2016). Under the Regular Credit method (effective since January 1, 2008), Indiana applies a tiered credit rate of 15 percent on the first $1,000,000 of excess Indiana QREs over the Indiana base amount (yielding up to $150,000), plus 10 percent on excess Indiana QREs above $1,000,000 (or for expenses after December 31, 2009, taxpayers may elect a 10 percent Alternative Simplified Credit on Indiana QREs exceeding 50 percent of the prior 3-year average, with a 5 percent fallback if any of the prior 3 years had zero QREs; unused credits are nonrefundable and carry forward up to 10 years). In administrative protests published in the Indiana Register, the Indiana Department of Revenue routinely cites Lafayette Square Amoco, Inc. v. Indiana Dep't of State Revenue (for the taxpayer's statutory burden under IC § 6-8.1-5-1(c)), Stinson Estate v. United States, 214 F.3d 846, 848 (7th Cir. 2000) (strict construction of tax credits), and Fudim v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 1994-235 (1994) to disallow unsubstantiated testimonial wage allocations.

In Idaho (Idaho Code § 63-3029G) the statute provides a nonrefundable credit equal to 5 percent on the excess of Idaho QREs over the predetermined Idaho base amount, subject to the 50 percent minimum base floor (so excess QREs cannot exceed 50 percent of current-year Idaho QREs). Under IC § 63-3029G(2)(b)(i), a taxpayer's gross receipts for the base amount include only gross receipts attributable to Idaho sources under IC § 63-3027(q) and (r). In Docket No. 0-723-166-208, the Idaho State Tax Commission strictly applied T.D. 9104, Union Carbide, and Max v. Commissioner to software development claims, distinguishing qualifying technical software development uncertainty resolved through a process of experimentation from non-qualifying business uncertainties (market reaction or product competitiveness) and project uncertainties (staff training or schedule/budget constraints).

In Arizona (A.R.S. § 43-1168 [Corporate] & § 43-1074.01 [Individual]) the state conforms to the federal IRC § 41 incremental base amount framework (and allows an ASC election) for research conducted in Arizona, applying a two-tiered credit rate structure. For taxable years 2011 through 2030, the credit equals 24 percent on the first $2,500,000 of excess Arizona QREs over the base amount (yielding up to $600,000), plus 15 percent on excess Arizona QREs exceeding $2,500,000. For taxable years 2031 and thereafter (post-2030 step-down), the statutory rates are scheduled to decrease to 20 percent on the first $2,500,000 of excess Arizona QREs (yielding up to $500,000), plus 11 percent on excess Arizona QREs exceeding $2,500,000. Unused credits carry forward for 10 consecutive years for tax years after 2021, and qualifying small businesses employing fewer than 150 full-time employees may apply to the ACA under A.R.S. § 41-1507 for a 75 percent partial refund of current-year excess credits (up to $100,000 per taxpayer per year under a $5,000,000 annual statewide cap).

In New Jersey (N.J.S.A. 54:10A-5.24) the state allows a Corporation Business Tax (CBT) credit equal to 10 percent of the excess of New Jersey QREs over the New Jersey base amount, plus 10 percent of basic research payments (all restricted to research conducted in New Jersey and computed in accordance with IRC § 41, with a 7-year carryforward, or 15 years for certain specified fields). (Proposed 2026 legislation S3560 would increase the QRE credit rate to 15 percent for taxpayers primarily engaged in targeted industries and 15 percent for all basic research payments, and allow unused credits to be claimed as a refundable overpayment.) New Jersey restricts the credit strictly to corporations under the CBT; partnerships are ineligible, and New Jersey S corporations can apply the credit only against entity-level New Jersey CBT liability and cannot pass the credit through to individual shareholders.

In Connecticut (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 12-217j [Incremental] & § 12-217n [Non-Incremental]) the state offers C corporations an incremental Research and Experimental Expenditures Tax Credit (Form CT-1120RC) under Conn. Gen. Stat. § 12-217j equal to 20 percent of the excess of current-year Connecticut research and experimental expenditures (defined under IRC § 174) over the base amount, where the base amount is defined simply as the amount spent on Connecticut research and experimental expenditures during the single immediately preceding income year. While the credit carries forward for 15 successive income years (with a 65 percent cash refund exchange available to qualified small businesses), utilization in any tax year is capped at a statutory percentage of total Corporation Business Tax due—specifically 60 percent of tax due in income year 2022, and 70 percent of tax due in income year 2023 and thereafter. (Connecticut also offers a separate non-incremental tiered credit from 1% to 6% under Conn. Gen. Stat. § 12-217n.)

In Rhode Island (R.I. Gen. Laws § 44-32-3) the state's Research and Development Expense Credit under R.I. Gen. Laws § 44-32-3 conforms to the federal 26 U.S.C. § 41 definitions of QREs and base period research expenses (for expenses incurred in Rhode Island after July 1, 1994) and applies a bifurcated rate structure to excess QREs over the base amount: 22.5 percent on the first $111,111 of excess Rhode Island QREs over the base amount (generating up to $25,000 in tax credit, as $111,111 × 22.5% = $24,999.98 ≈ $25,000), and 16.9 percent on all remaining excess Rhode Island QREs above $111,111. The credit cannot reduce corporate tax liability by more than 50 percent (or below the minimum corporate tax under R.I. Gen. Laws § 44-11-2(e)), has a 7-year carryforward, and effective January 1, 2011, is disallowed against the Rhode Island personal income tax (Chapter 44-30).
Hypothetical Worked Algebraic Applications of the Base Amount

To demonstrate the exact mathematical interaction among the fixed-base percentage, four-year average gross receipts, the 50 percent minimum floor, and state-specific base modifications, the following three hypothetical worked examples are computed step by step against the statutory formulas.
Hypothetical Example 1: Standard Federal Base Amount Where the Revenue-Scaled Hurdle Exceeds Current QREs

Assume a hypothetical mature domestic aerospace manufacturing corporation has a verified and consistent Fixed-Base Percentage (FBP) of 8.00% based on its 1984–1988 aggregate QREs and gross receipts (well below the 16.00% statutory ceiling of 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(C)). In the current credit year, the corporation incurs $2,000,000 in qualified research expenses (comprising in-house wages, supplies, and 65% of eligible contract research per IRC § 41(b)). Over the four preceding taxable years, its net gross receipts (after excluding returns, allowances, and capital asset sales per 26 CFR § 1.41-3(c)(2)) were $40,000,000 (Year -1), $38,000,000 (Year -2), $35,000,000 (Year -3), and $31,000,000 (Year -4).

In Step 1, computing the prior four-year average annual gross receipts under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(1)(B) by summing the four preceding years' gross receipts ($40,000,000 + $38,000,000 + $35,000,000 + $31,000,000 = $144,000,000) and dividing by 4 yields $36,000,000. In Step 2, multiplying the 8.00% FBP by $36,000,000 in average annual gross receipts under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(1) yields a preliminary calculated base amount of $2,880,000. In Step 3, multiplying 50% by $2,000,000 in credit-year QREs under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(2) yields a minimum base amount floor of $1,000,000. In Step 4, taking the greater of the preliminary base amount ($2,880,000) and the 50% minimum floor ($1,000,000) establishes an effective base amount of $2,880,000. Because current-year QREs ($2,000,000) do not exceed $2,880,000, excess QREs equal $0 and the resulting federal Regular Research Credit under 26 U.S.C. § 41(a)(1) is $0.

body.text: Analytical Takeaway: When a mature company experiences substantial revenue expansion over the preceding four years while its R&D budget remains flat, its revenue-indexed base amount ($2,880,000) outstrips its current QREs ($2,000,000), yielding $0 under the Regular Research Credit method (which is why such taxpayers typically elect the Alternative Simplified Credit under IRC § 41(c)(4)).
Hypothetical Example 2: California Zero Gross Receipts Base Amount (FTB LDG 2012-03-01)

Assume a hypothetical early-stage software start-up conducts 100 percent of its software engineering in San Jose, California, incurring $1,500,000 in California QREs during the credit year, but licenses and delivers its cloud-based SaaS platform exclusively to commercial customers located in New York and Europe. Under Cal. R&TC § 23609(i) (formerly § 23609(h)(3)), because it has no sales of property delivered or shipped to purchasers within California (and service/licensing receipts are excluded), its California gross receipts for the four preceding taxable years are $0.

In Step 1, multiplying the 3.00% start-up FBP by $0 in average California gross receipts yields a raw calculated base amount of $0 (note that even if the taxpayer were in its 6th+ credit year where division by zero defaults the FBP to 16.00% per Form FTB 3523 instructions and IRC § 41(c)(3)(C), 16.00% multiplied by $0 still equals $0). In Step 2, applying the mandatory 50 percent minimum base amount floor under FTB LDG 2012-03-01 and IRC § 41(c)(2) by taking the greater of $0 and 50% of $1,500,000 in current-year California QREs establishes an effective California base amount of $750,000. In Step 3, subtracting the $750,000 effective base amount from $1,500,000 in current-year California QREs leaves $750,000 in excess California QREs; multiplying $750,000 by California's 15% statutory rate yields a California Regular Research Credit of $112,500 (an effective credit rate of 7.50% of total California QREs, as $112,500 ÷ $1,500,000 = 7.50%).

body.text: Hypothetical Example 3: Pennsylvania Small Business Base Amount

Assume a hypothetical pre-revenue biotechnology company operating a research laboratory in Philadelphia has $3,000,000 in net book value of total assets (qualifying as a small business under Pennsylvania's $5,000,000 asset ceiling). In the current credit year, the company incurs $800,000 in Pennsylvania QREs (laboratory supplies and chemist wages performed in Pennsylvania), and over the four immediately preceding taxable years its average annual Pennsylvania QREs were $500,000 (satisfying the mandatory two-year prior Pennsylvania R&D expenditure history requirement).

In Step 1, multiplying 50% by $800,000 in current-year Pennsylvania QREs yields a 50 percent minimum floor of $400,000. In Step 2, comparing the prior four-year average Pennsylvania QREs ($500,000) against the 50% floor ($400,000) establishes a Pennsylvania base amount of $500,000. In Step 3, subtracting the $500,000 base amount from $800,000 in current-year Pennsylvania QREs yields $300,000 in excess Pennsylvania QREs; applying the 20% small business credit rate to $300,000 yields a tentative Pennsylvania R&D credit of $60,000 (whereas if the company's net book value of assets were $5,000,000 or greater, the standard 10 percent rate would apply, yielding a tentative credit of $30,000 before any statewide cap proration).
